body:
For characters that are not in Unicode, there’s the Private Use Area, but the public Web isn’t a private system. A font is likely to work visually depending on the characteristics of the script, but doesn’t work for purposes other than visual rendering.

To establish non-private identity of characters in non-proprietary writing systems used by a user community (other than fandom of a proprietary work of fiction), the correct way is to get the characters encoded in Unicode. This takes time, and the situation is bad until the process has run its course, but with a long-term view, it would be worse for the WHATWG to steer these language communities to settle on something less.

For scripts that Unicode has rejected (notably scripts associated with a proprietary work of fiction), that avenue isn’t available, but WHATWG isn’t better positioned to standardize what Unicode has documented reasons not to standardize.

For languages written in scripts other than their most likely script, there is already a standardized solution: You can use the [script subtag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Script_(Unicode)) in the `lang` attribute: `ja-Latn` for Japanese in the Latin script or `en-Dsrt` for English in the Deseret script.
